Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

displayContent.text:
# Plan: rate limiting for the orders API

One customer's script created 40,000 orders in ten minutes last week and slowed every other customer down. I want to add rate limiting to `src/server.ts` and ship it this week.

What we have:

- 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer.
- A Redis 7 cluster already used for sessions by another service; we may use it.
- `POST /orders` writes to Postgres and is the expensive call; `GET /orders` is cheap.
- About 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.

Not decided yet:

- What to key the limit on: `x-customer-id`, client IP, or both.
- Algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, or token bucket.
- Where counters live: Redis, or in each instance's memory.
- What happens if the counter store is unreachable: let requests through or reject them.
- How enterprise customers get higher limits, and who owns those numbers.
- What a rejected client sees.
- How to roll it out without breaking the enterprise integrations.

questions.question: What should the rate limit key on?

options.label: x-customer-id only
options.tradeoff: Matches the existing auth header; lets you set per-customer limits and exempt/raise limits for known enterprise customers. Loses protection against a single customer spreading requests across many identities.
options.description: Use the `x-customer-id` header as the rate-limit key.

options.label: client IP only
options.tradeoff: Simple, but NAT/proxies/LB mean many real customers may share an IP and one customer with multiple egress IPs gets multiple limits.
options.description: Use the connecting client IP as the rate-limit key.

options.label: Both x-customer-id and IP
options.tradeoff: Most precise, but doubles counter state and makes enterprise-limit policy harder to express.
options.description: Rate-limit per (customer-id, IP) pair.

brief.where: `src/server.ts` already requires and reads `x-customer-id` for every request. The service runs 3 instances behind a round-robin load balancer, and about 20 enterprise customers have scripted integrations that legitimately burst.
brief.what: The rate limit needs a key to bucket requests. The choice determines whether an enterprise customer can be identified for higher limits and whether a distributed attacker is still a problem.
brief.how: After you pick the key, the next round can nail down how enterprise customers get higher limits. If the key cannot identify customers, that branch of the design tree changes shape.

options.label: Fixed window
options.tradeoff: Very simple to implement and reason about, but allows a burst of 2× the limit at window boundaries and can stampede all instances at the reset instant.
options.description: Allow N requests per fixed time window (e.g. 1000 orders per minute), resetting at each window boundary.

options.label: Sliding window
options.tradeoff: Smoothes boundary bursts, but requires more Redis operations or keeping a request log per key.
options.description: Allow N requests in the last W seconds, recomputed for every request.

options.label: Token bucket
options.tradeoff: Natural fit for bursty scripted integrations; lets you grant a large burst capacity while capping long-term rate. Slightly more state to manage (bucket level).
options.description: Each customer has a bucket with capacity B; tokens refill at rate R per second; each request consumes one token.

brief.where: The incident was 40,000 orders in 10 minutes. About 20 enterprise customers legitimately burst. The limit needs to stop sustained abuse without breaking normal batch behavior.
brief.what: The algorithm determines how aggressively one customer can burst, how smooth the limit is, and how complex the Redis/memory implementation will be.
brief.how: The choice affects the shape of the enterprise-limit policy and the counter-store design. Token bucket and sliding window give better burst control; fixed window is simplest.

questions.question: Where should the rate-limit counters live?

options.label: Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Correctly shares state across all 3 instances, so one customer cannot get 3× the limit by round-robining. Adds a network hop and a dependency that can fail.
options.description: Store counters in the existing Redis 7 cluster.

options.label: In-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: Fast and no new dependency, but with 3 round-robin instances a customer effectively gets 3× the limit and one hot customer can still starve others on the same instance.
options.description: Store counters in each `src/server.ts` process.

brief.where: There are 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer, and a Redis 7 cluster is already used for sessions by another service.
brief.what: Counter location determines consistency across instances, failure modes, and whether the chosen algorithm behaves the same everywhere.
brief.how: If you pick Redis, the next round must decide the unreachable-store fallback. If you pick in-memory, that branch closes and rollout needs sticky sessions or acceptance of the 3× limit.

questions.question: What should a rejected client receive?

options.label: HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header and a plain-text body
options.tradeoff: Standard, easy for scripts to handle, and matches the existing plain-text error responses in `src/server.ts`. Does not expose the current limit budget.
options.description: Return status 429, set `Retry-After: <seconds>`, body like `rate limit exceeded`.

options.label: HTTP 429 with a JSON error body including `retryAfter`
options.tradeoff: More structured for scripted integrations, but introduces JSON error bodies that the rest of the app does not yet use.
options.description: Return status 429, body like `{"error":"rate limit exceeded","retryAfter":<seconds>}`.

options.label: HTTP 429 with no extra headers
options.tradeoff: Minimal, but scripts have no signal for when to retry, increasing retry storms.
options.description: Return status 429 and a short body only.

options.label: HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Wrong semantics: 503 implies server overload, not client excess. May confuse monitoring and retries.
options.description: Return status 503 when a customer exceeds their limit.

brief.where: `src/server.ts` currently returns plain-text errors (`missing x-customer-id` as 401, `not found` as 404). Clients are scripted integrations, not browsers.
brief.what: The response shape determines how easily scripts can back off and whether monitoring treats rejections correctly.
brief.how: The choice is independent of key/algorithm/store, but the response format must be stable before rollout so enterprise customers can update their scripts.

brief.what: The algorithm determines how aggressively one customer can burst, how smooth the limit is, and how complex the Redis/memory implementation will be.
brief.how: The choice affects the shape of the enterprise-limit policy and the counter-store design. Token bucket and sliding window give better burst control; fixed window is simplest.

questions.question: Where should the rate-limit counters live?

options.label: Redis cluster
options.tradeoff: Correctly shares state across all 3 instances, so one customer cannot get 3× the limit by round-robining. Adds a network hop and a dependency that can fail.
options.description: Store counters in the existing Redis 7 cluster.

options.label: In-memory per instance
options.tradeoff: Fast and no new dependency, but with 3 round-robin instances a customer effectively gets 3× the limit and one hot customer can still starve others on the same instance.
options.description: Store counters in each `src/server.ts` process.

brief.where: There are 3 instances of `src/server.ts` behind a round-robin load balancer, and a Redis 7 cluster is already used for sessions by another service.
brief.what: Counter location determines consistency across instances, failure modes, and whether the chosen algorithm behaves the same everywhere.
brief.how: If you pick Redis, the next round must decide the unreachable-store fallback. If you pick in-memory, that branch closes and rollout needs sticky sessions or acceptance of the 3× limit.

questions.question: What should a rejected client receive?

options.label: HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header and a plain-text body
options.tradeoff: Standard, easy for scripts to handle, and matches the existing plain-text error responses in `src/server.ts`. Does not expose the current limit budget.
options.description: Return status 429, set `Retry-After: <seconds>`, body like `rate limit exceeded`.

options.label: HTTP 429 with a JSON error body including `retryAfter`
options.tradeoff: More structured for scripted integrations, but introduces JSON error bodies that the rest of the app does not yet use.
options.description: Return status 429, body like `{"error":"rate limit exceeded","retryAfter":<seconds>}`.

options.label: HTTP 429 with no extra headers
options.tradeoff: Minimal, but scripts have no signal for when to retry, increasing retry storms.
options.description: Return status 429 and a short body only.

options.label: HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
options.tradeoff: Wrong semantics: 503 implies server overload, not client excess. May confuse monitoring and retries.
options.description: Return status 503 when a customer exceeds their limit.

brief.where: `src/server.ts` currently returns plain-text errors (`missing x-customer-id` as 401, `not found` as 404). Clients are scripted integrations, not browsers.
brief.what: The response shape determines how easily scripts can back off and whether monitoring treats rejections correctly.
brief.how: The choice is independent of key/algorithm/store, but the response format must be stable before rollout so enterprise customers can update their scripts.
